lesson.title: Trust but Verify: The Habit That Catches Mistakes
lesson.summary: Learn the habit and method of checking a solution by substitution, confirming it satisfies the original equation and catching arithmetic slips before they become wrong answers.
lesson.body:
Every worked example throughout this unit ended with the same move: substituting the found value back into the original equation to confirm both sides came out equal. Checking a solution is not an optional extra step tacked onto the end of solving; it is how you know, with certainty rather than hope, that the value you found actually belongs to the equation's solution set. Arithmetic slips, sign errors, and dropped terms are common while solving multi-step equations, especially ones involving fractions, decimals, or variables on both sides, and checking is the reliable way to catch them before they cause a wrong answer to be trusted.

The method itself relies directly on substitution: replace every occurrence of the variable in the original, unsimplified equation with the value you solved for, then simplify each side completely and separately, using the order of operations. If the two sides simplify to the same number, the solution checks out. It is important to substitute into the original equation as it was first written, not into some simplified or partially solved version, since an error made early in the solving process would otherwise be checked against itself and go unnoticed.

Suppose solving 3(x - 2) + 5 = 2x + 3 produced x = 2 as a candidate answer. Substitute x = 2 into the left side: 3(2 - 2) + 5 = 3(0) + 5 = 0 + 5 = 5. Substitute x = 2 into the right side: 2(2) + 3 = 4 + 3 = 7. The two sides come out to 5 and 7, which are not equal, so x = 2 does not check, revealing that a mistake occurred somewhere in the solving process. Solving the equation correctly instead: distribute the left side to get 3x - 6 + 5 = 2x + 3, which simplifies to 3x - 1 = 2x + 3; subtract 2x from both sides to get x - 1 = 3, then add 1 to both sides to get x = 4. Checking x = 4: left side is 3(4 - 2) + 5 = 3(2) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11, and right side is 2(4) + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11. Both sides equal 11, confirming x = 4 is the correct solution.

Checking a solution only makes sense because of what a variable represents: a placeholder for the one specific number that makes a true statement, so plugging in a candidate value and testing for equality is a direct test of the definition itself. The same substitution habit extends naturally to the special cases covered in this unit: for a conditional equation, exactly one value should check successfully; for a contradiction, no value will ever check, since the solution set is empty; and for an identity, any value at all will check, since the solution set is every real number.

Making a habit of checking every solution, even ones that seem obviously correct, catches errors early and builds genuine confidence in an answer rather than a guess about whether it is right. It costs only a minute of substitution and simplification, and it is the single most reliable safeguard against turning a small arithmetic slip into a wrong final answer.
